e.meaning: feminine form of Carl, free man
e.etymology: A spelling of Carly, a pet form of Carla and Carol and so a feminine of Carl and Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man.
From Old High German wolf, wolf, and gang, path or course. It has been in use since the 8th century and was the name of a 10th-century saint, the bishop of Regensburg.
namesakes: Wolfgang Van Halen (rock musician, son of Eddie Van Halen)

assoc.t: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, the composer
Wolfgang Puck, celebrity chef and restaurateur

e.etymology: A respelling of Grayson, an English surname meaning son of the greyve, a northern word for a steward or bailiff. Most people now hear the color gray in it.
The Spanish and Italian form of Rudolph, through Latin Rudolphus, from Germanic words for fame and wolf. Film idol Rudolph Valentino was born Rodolfo.
namesakes: Rodolfo (the poet hero of Puccini's opera La Bohème)

e.meaning: nobleman ranking just below a duke
e.etymology: The French noble title marquis, originally the lord of a march or border territory. US parents have used it since the 1800s; it rose in the late 20th century, mainly in African American families.

assoc.t: marquis, a rank of European nobility

e.etymology: A spelling of Derek, which English borrowed in the Middle Ages from a Low German form of Theodoric, ruler of the people, and revived in the 19th century.
The Hebrew form of Joel, Yo'el, the Lord is God, the name of one of the twelve minor prophets. The Y spelling is used in Israel and is also common among Cuban families.

e.meaning: short form of Cameron, Gaelic for crooked nose
e.etymology: A shortening of Cameron, a Scottish clan name from Gaelic cam, crooked, and sròn, nose. It also shortens Camden and Camilla, and Cam is a separate Vietnamese given name.
namesakes: Cam Ward (quarterback taken first in the 2025 NFL draft)
Cam Tucker (Eric Stonestreet's character on Modern Family)

assoc.t: cam, short for camera, as in webcam; also an engine part

e.meaning: pet form of Isabella, Isaac and other Is- names
e.etymology: A pet form of names beginning Is- or Iz-: Isabel and Isabella, forms of Elizabeth, for girls; Isaac, Israel, Isaiah and Isidore for boys.
namesakes: Izzy Stradlin (founding guitarist of Guns N' Roses)
Izzy Moonbow (unicorn in My Little Pony: A New Generation)

e.etymology: The everyday short form of Chevrolet, the car brand named for Swiss-born racing driver Louis Chevrolet. Comedian Chevy Chase's nickname comes instead from the old border ballad of Chevy Chase.
namesakes: Chevy Chase (comedian of Saturday Night Live and the Vacation films)

assoc.t: Chevy, short for Chevrolet, GM's car and truck brand
Chevy Chase, comedian and actor

e.etymology: From Arabic nur, light. The Light is one of the names of God in Islam and the title of sura 24 of the Quran. Nour is the French-influenced spelling used in Lebanon, Egypt and North Africa.

e.meaning: lord, a form of address for a king
e.etymology: The English word sire, the old form of address for a king, from Old French sire and Latin senior, elder. It joined King, Royal and Reign as a title name in the 2010s.

assoc.t: sire, address for a king; as a verb, to father offspring
Sire Records, label of Madonna and the Ramones

e.etymology: The Spanish, Italian and Polish spelling of Lydia, Greek for a woman from Lydia, an ancient kingdom in western Asia Minor. In Acts, Lydia of Thyatira is an early convert baptized by Paul.
namesakes: Lidia Bastianich (Italian American chef and public television host)

e.etymology: A respelling of Presley, an English surname from a place name, Old English preost, priest, and leah, meadow or clearing. As a first name it follows the fame of Elvis Presley.

assoc.t: Elvis Presley, the King of Rock and Roll

e.etymology: Latin draco, from Greek drakon, a dragon or great serpent. It was the name of a 7th-century BC Athenian lawgiver whose harsh code gave English the word draconian.

assoc.t: Draco Malfoy, Harry Potter's rival at Hogwarts
Draco, the dragon constellation of the northern sky
Draco, a compact AK-style pistol often named in rap

e.etymology: Created for Winry Rockbell, the mechanic heroine of the Japanese manga and anime Fullmetal Alchemist, which began in 2001. It has no earlier history as a given name.

assoc.t: Winry Rockbell, heroine of Fullmetal Alchemist

e.etymology: A Japanese name most often understood as nami, wave. It can also be written with characters chosen for their sound, such as na with mi, beauty.

assoc.t: Nami, navigator of the Straw Hat Pirates in One Piece
NAMI, the National Alliance on Mental Illness
Nami, a mermaid champion in League of Legends

e.etymology: A Spanish contraction of María Isabel. María is from Hebrew Miriam, and Isabel is the medieval Spanish form of Elizabeth, my God is an oath.

e.meaning: from an Irish surname meaning descendant of Bradán, salmon
e.etymology: A modern spelling of Braden, a surname from Irish Ó Bradáin, descendant of Bradán, a byname meaning salmon. The many Brayden spellings rose with Aiden and Jayden in the 2000s.
A modern American compound of Blake and the -lynn ending. Blake is an English surname from Old English blaec, dark, or blac, pale.

Sanskrit samadhi, complete meditative absorption, the last of the eight limbs of yoga and a core term in Buddhism. As a girls' name it is used in Latin America, as by Mexican actress Samadhi Zendejas.
e.note: In India samadhi also means a memorial shrine or tomb of a revered person.

e.meaning: pet form of Samuel, heard by God
e.etymology: A pet form of Sam, short for Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, usually read as name of God or God has heard, and for Samantha. It is also an English spelling of the Arabic name Sami.
namesakes: Sammy Davis Jr. (Rat Pack singer and entertainer)

assoc.t: sammy or sammie, slang for a sandwich

e.etymology: From Arabic na'ila, one who attains or achieves, the feminine of Nail. An early bearer was Naila, wife of the caliph Uthman. In the US the name is well established in African American families.
The South Slavic form of Nicholas, from Greek Nikolaos, built from nike, victory, and laos, people. It is a man's name in Serbia, Croatia and Bulgaria.
namesakes: Nikola Jokić (Denver Nuggets center and three-time NBA MVP)
e.note: In Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Nikola is mainly a girls' name.

assoc.t: Nikola Tesla, electrical inventor
Nikola Jokic, three-time NBA Most Valuable Player

e.etymology: A form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious', by way of Greek and Latin Johannes. It is a French spelling beside Yoann and Johan, and the Korean form of the biblical John.
A clipped respelling of Crew, the English word name that rose in the 2010s. Cru is also the French wine term for a vineyard or growth, as in grand cru.

assoc.t: French wine term for a vineyard, as in grand cru
Cru, the campus ministry once called Campus Crusade

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Nathan, favored by Spanish-speaking families because it writes the English pronunciation the Spanish way. Nathan is Hebrew for 'he gave'; the prophet Nathan advised King David.
A respelling of Laken, a name, perhaps suggested by the word lake, that spread in the 1980s through the character Laken Lockridge on the soap opera Santa Barbara.
From an English surname, a variant of Massey, which came from Norman French place names. As a girls' name it is a modern spelling alongside Macy.

assoc.t: sounds like Macy's, the department store chain

e.etymology: Short form of Vincent, from the Latin name Vincentius, built on vincere, 'to conquer'. It was common as a name in its own right in the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Vince Lombardi (Hall of Fame Green Bay Packers coach)

assoc.t: Vince, upscale clothing label

e.meaning: Mecca, the holiest city of Islam
e.etymology: From the city in Saudi Arabia, Arabic Makka, birthplace of Muhammad and destination of the hajj. The origin of the place name is uncertain. As a given name it is mostly American.

assoc.t: Mecca, Islam's holiest city, in Saudi Arabia
a mecca: a place that draws devotees of something

e.meaning: from a Germanic name built on the word for battle
e.etymology: Spanish form of the medieval Latin Gundisalvus, a Visigothic name whose first element is Germanic gunth, 'battle'; the second is uncertain. It honors Saint Gonzalo, an 11th-century Galician bishop.
